text: Lesson 6 covered LP tokens: deposit two assets into an AMM pool, get a token representing your share, earn a cut of trading fees. A yield farm adds a second layer — stake that LP token into a rewards contract, and the protocol emits its own token to you on top of the fees you're already earning.

That creates two income streams with very different risk profiles. Trading fees are real revenue, paid in the pool's actual assets, roughly proportional to volume. Emission rewards are newly minted tokens whose dollar value depends entirely on that token holding its price under constant sell pressure from farmers cashing out.

Farm APY is annual reward value in dollars, divided by total value locked, times 100. A farm emitting 2 million dollars a year into a pool with 10 million TVL advertises 20%. But that number is only as real as the reward token's price — if it halves, the effective APY anyone actually earns is already cut in half.

The virtuous version of this loop: emit rewards, attract LPs, deepen liquidity, lower slippage, generate more trading volume and fee revenue. It breaks when emissions are the only reason LPs showed up — farmers deposit purely for the reward, sell it immediately, the price falls, the advertised APY falls, and they withdraw for the next farm.

That's mercenary capital — liquidity with no loyalty to the protocol, present only because the yield is temporarily highest. It arrives fast when emissions start and leaves just as fast when a competing farm offers a better rate, taking the protocol's liquidity depth with it.

Durable designs fight this with vesting on reward claims, tapering emission schedules, and a real-yield component that keeps some return alive even if the reward token's price falls to zero. Next: vaults, and how auto-compounding builds directly on top of what you just saw.
